summary: An independent reviewer (a separate AI model that never saw the tool's answers) checked all 54 bills from the raw records, and a person then confirmed every contested call. First pass: 46 of 54 agreed (85%). Of the 8 differences, 7 were rule errors we fixed and 1 we kept on purpose. The 2 misses we found ourselves were fixed before the review ran, so the very first version would have agreed on at most 44. After the fixes, 53 of 54 agree (98%), on the same bills the rules were fixed against, so that is not a fresh-data score: the shadow week measures that.

entries.why: Two months before this bill they complained to the state consumer affairs office and threatened to contest the card charge. The tool only linked tickets raised after the bill.
entries.change: A chargeback, regulator or legal threat in the last 180 days stops chasing until the account manager and Head of Support say it's settled.

entries.why: They opened chargebacks on two payments on 2 July, one day outside the first 120-day window.
entries.change: Same rule, with a 180-day window as a setting.

entries.foundBy: Our own check, before the review (shown to Maya)
entries.why: The ticket named this invoice and refused to pay for a cancelled module, but the rules read "cancellation" as an escalation, so the tool said call.
entries.change: A ticket naming an unpaid bill is a dispute, whatever else it says. Every call shows the customer's tickets beside it.

entries.foundBy: Our own check, before the review (shown to Maya)
entries.why: "Late fee should not be there": the word "outage" made it an escalation, so the dispute was missed. Only the top-50 rule caught it.
Only 4 days late; the first reminder goes at day 7.
entries.change: Bills under 7 days late wait until day 7.

entries.why: The same customer also gets a call about an 83-day bill: an email and a call on the same day.
entries.change: One conversation per customer: other bills go on the same call.

entries.foundBy: Independent review, after a rule change
entries.why: Two days earlier they asked where an approved duplicate-charge refund was. A rule change briefly let a reminder through; the review caught it before any version went out.
entries.change: A money complaint from the last 30 days holds the bill, even when Zendesk marks it solved.

entries.why: The "pending" ticket's last message from the customer was "Closing this out".
entries.change: When the customer says it's resolved, the ticket stops blocking.

entries.why: A normal-priority question, pending since July: support is waiting on the customer.
entries.change: My call, for Maya to confirm: a pending ticket pauses the reminder only if it's about money, urgent, or waiting on us. Otherwise a softer reminder, and the account manager is told.

entries.why: A pending timer bug, tagged How-to by mistake. Not about money.
entries.change: Same call as Kingsway, for Maya to confirm.

entries.why: The reviewer would send: the open ticket is a product question. The tool holds because it's open and waiting on Ledgerline.
entries.change: Kept on purpose: a ticket waiting on us still pauses the reminder, and it's a top-50 account, so a person reads it anyway.

entries.foundBy: Second look at the hand check
entries.why: One $5,100 payment with a blank memo, two $5,100 bills. The tool assumed it paid the older one, so the newer one would have got a reminder. My hand check passed it.
entries.change: The second bill now waits for Marcus, who is asked which bill the payment covers. The label was updated to match.

entries.why: Customers also email billing@ in Gmail. Disputes sent there are invisible to the tool.
entries.change: Next: read the billing@ inbox (Google is already a vendor).
